quotes.text: The trust runs in one direction, because the rule was published in advance for the whole world to see. SPF is a domain saying in public, here is exactly who is allowed to speak.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains SPF in one plain-language image.

quotes.text: This is where DKIM beats SPF because the seal travels with the message. It usually survives forwarding, which is the very thing that breaks SPF.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Pinpoints the key practical difference between DKIM and SPF.

quotes.text: None is a watchtower. Quarantine is a warning label and reject is a locked door. The skill isn't choosing the toughest one. The skill is knowing when to move to the next one.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Memorable metaphor for the three DMARC policies and the rollout mindset.

quotes.text: Every step gives you information that makes the next step safer. Skip ahead and you're guessing about your own mail streams, and guessing is how a real invoice ends up in a spam folder.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clear argument for a staged email authentication rollout.

The right order to roll this out

takeaways: SPF lists who may send for your domain, DKIM proves a message was not altered, and DMARC checks that one of them aligns with the visible From domain.
Roll out in order: SPF with soft fail, DKIM with both selector records in Microsoft 365, DMARC at none with reports, then quarantine and finally reject.
Custom domains in Microsoft 365 are not DKIM-signed until you enable it, a domain must publish only one DMARC record, and monitoring at none alone is not protection.
hook: Anyone can send email that pretends to be your company, and Business Email Compromise turns that gap into real losses. This Simply Explained episode is for Microsoft 365 admins and IT teams responsible for their mail domains. It explains SPF, DKIM and DMARC in plain words and gives a safe order to roll them out without blocking your own mail.
